conversation.subtopic: Atypical presentations of abdominal conditions and their diagnostic challenges

conversation.content:
I once saw a patient with “gastritis” symptoms who turned out to have acute coronary syndrome—troponin was elevated, and the ECG showed subtle ischemic changes.  
Another case involved a young woman with right lower quadrant pain initially thought to be appendicitis, but it was actually a ruptured ovarian cyst mimicking peritonitis.  
In one baffling instance, a man’s chronic epigastric discomfort was traced back to a thoracic aortic aneurysm compressing nearby nerves.  
When labs and imaging are normal, I always consider cardiac, pulmonary, or even musculoskeletal referrals—especially if the pain doesn’t fit classic patterns.  
The key is keeping a broad differential and not stopping at the obvious, even when initial tests seem reassuring.
conversation.subtopic: Atypical presentations of abdominal conditions and their diagnostic challenges

conversation.content:
I’ve seen cases where abdominal pain was actually due to spinal issues—like a herniated disc at L1-L2 referring pain to the epigastrium, mimicking peptic ulcer disease.  
One patient spent months on PPIs before an MRI revealed nerve root compression; once treated, the “abdominal” pain vanished.  
It’s easy to overlook musculoskeletal or neurological causes when we’re laser-focused on GI or vascular etiologies.  
I now routinely ask about posture changes, back pain, or radicular symptoms—even if they seem unrelated.  
Sometimes the most elusive diagnoses hide in plain sight, masked by textbook presentations that don’t quite fit.  
A thorough neurologic exam and targeted imaging can uncover what standard abdominal workups miss.  
Never assume normal labs mean benign—it might just mean you’re looking in the wrong place.
conversation.subtopic: Atypical presentations of abdominal conditions and their diagnostic challenges

conversation.content:
I remember a patient with vague left upper quadrant pain dismissed as gastritis—turns out it was splenic infarction from atrial fibrillation, picked up only after an echocardiogram revealed a clot.  
Another time, a teenager’s “IBS-like” cramps were actually due to lead poisoning from inherited paint exposure—blood lead levels were sky-high, and abdominal X-ray showed radiopaque particles.  
I’ve also seen diabetic autonomic neuropathy masquerade as chronic constipation and bloating, with no structural cause found until gastric emptying studies confirmed gastroparesis.  
One of the trickiest was a woman with cyclical lower abdominal pain diagnosed as endometriosis—until laparoscopy showed nothing, and further workup revealed a rare pelvic venous plexus varicosity causing referred pain.  
These cases taught me that normal CT or ultrasound doesn’t equal normal pathology—it just means you haven’t asked the right question yet.  
Always consider systemic illnesses, toxins, or neurologic dysfunction when GI-focused tests come back clean.  
The more atypical the presentation, the more you need to think beyond the abdomen—even if it hurts there.  
Sometimes the real diagnosis is hiding in plain sight, but only if you’re willing to look sideways.

conversation.content:
I’ve seen too many young patients with epigastric pain dismissed as “stress” or “indigestion” only to later discover silent myocardial ischemia—especially in women or those without traditional risk factors.  
You’d be surprised how often a simple ECG or troponin ordered on a hunch changes everything, even when the patient is 30 and runs marathons.  
When the pain doesn’t localize or respond to GI meds, I push for thoracic imaging or spine MRI early—not waiting for red flags, because by then, it’s often too late.  
Systemic causes like lead poisoning or autoimmune disease? I start thinking about them the moment the history feels “off”—like symptoms worsening after meals but no acid reflux relief, or unexplained fatigue alongside bloating.  
Patients *do* drop clues: one woman mentioned her pain eased when lying flat—that turned out to be diaphragmatic irritation from a subphrenic abscess.  
My go-to next step when tests are normal but the story doesn’t add up? A detailed activity diary + targeted physical exam—sometimes palpating the costovertebral angle or checking for dermatomal patterns reveals more than any CT.  
Balancing urgency vs. overtesting? I anchor to clinical gestalt—if the patient looks ill or the pain is progressive, I escalate fast; if stable, I narrow the focus with serial exams and selective imaging.  
One pearl I now use religiously: always ask about recent travel, hobbies, or home renovations—those “irrelevant” details have uncovered everything from parasitic infections to heavy metal toxicity masquerading as IBS.

conversation.content:
Atypical abdominal presentations often stem from non-GI sources—cardiac, pulmonary, spinal, or even systemic toxins—and can easily mislead if you stop at normal imaging or labs.  
Cases like silent MI in young athletes, thoracic aneurysms mimicking gastritis, or lead poisoning masquerading as IBS show how critical it is to think beyond the abdomen.  
Neurologic referrals, like disc herniations causing epigastric pain, or pelvic varicosities mimicking endometriosis, highlight the value of targeted physical exams and MRI when red flags hint at deeper issues.  
Patients often drop subtle clues—posture changes, timing with meals, or activity triggers—that point to non-GI origins, so listening closely matters more than ordering another CT.  
Systemic causes should be considered early when symptoms feel “off,” especially if they don’t respond to standard GI treatments or come with unexplained fatigue or weight loss.  
I’ve learned to escalate quickly when clinical gestalt suggests something’s wrong—even without classic risk factors—because waiting for red flags can cost lives.  
My go-to move now? A detailed activity diary and focused physical exam, plus asking about travel, hobbies, or home renovations—they’ve uncovered diagnoses no lab would catch.  
The real lesson? Normal tests don’t mean benign; they just mean you haven’t asked the right question yet—and sometimes, the answer lies outside the belly.

conversation.content: I’ve started wondering how often we miss endocrine causes—like adrenal insufficiency or pheochromocytoma—when patients present with vague, waxing-and-waning abdominal pain that doesn’t fit any GI pattern. One case I saw involved a woman with recurrent nausea and cramping who’d been labeled “functional” until her cortisol levels crashed during a stress test; turns out she had Addison’s disease mimicking IBS. Another patient’s episodic hypertension and epigastric burning led us to a pheo after we noticed his pain spiked with palpitations—something we wouldn’t have caught if we hadn’t asked about symptom triggers. These endocrine culprits are sneaky because they don’t always scream “hormonal”—they whisper through fatigue, weight changes, or weird timing of symptoms. I now routinely check electrolytes and morning cortisol in anyone with unexplained chronic abdominal discomfort plus systemic red flags like orthostasis or salt cravings. It’s easy to write off these cases as psychosomatic when the CT is clean, but sometimes the real issue is hiding in the adrenal glands or pituitary—not the pancreas. And honestly, asking about stress levels or recent life upheavals can be more revealing than another ultrasound. You’d be surprised how many “gut problems” resolve once you treat the underlying hormonal imbalance. So yeah, next time someone’s belly pain feels oddly systemic, maybe look up—not just down.

I’d bet most clinicians still default to GI workups until the endocrine system screams loud enough to be heard.

It’s not just about ordering more tests, but rewiring our thinking to see systemic red flags as urgent clues, not background noise.  
We need to normalize checking cortisol and electrolytes early in “functional” cases—because sometimes the gut isn’t broken, the glands are.

I’m not convinced we’re actually doing better—we still default to “it’s stress” or “functional GI” until someone collapses or spikes a crazy BP.  
How many patients with salt cravings, fatigue, and vague cramps are still getting PPIs or antispasmodics instead of a morning cortisol?  
It’s easy to say “think endocrine” after the fact, but in real time, when you’re swamped and the CT’s clean, who’s really ordering catecholamines on a 28-year-old with “IBS”?

If we’re waiting for adrenal crisis to confirm Addison’s, we’ve already failed the patient.  
Maybe the problem isn’t lack of knowledge—it’s that we’re too comfortable letting normal imaging lull us into diagnostic complacency.  
Until we make endocrine screening routine in unexplained chronic abdominal pain, we’re still playing catch-up—not staying ahead.

Castel Nuovo (; "New Castle"), often called Maschio Angioino (; "Angevin Keep"), is a medieval castle located in front of Piazza Municipio and the city hall (Palazzo San Giacomo) in central Naples, Campania, Italy. Its scenic location and imposing size makes the castle, first erected in 1279, one of the main architectural landmarks of the city. It was a royal seat for kings of Naples, Aragon and Spain until 1815.

It is the headquarters of Società Napoletana di Storia Patria (Neapolitan Society of Homeland History) and of the Naples Committee of the Istituto per la storia del Risorgimento italiano (Institute for the History of the Italian Risorgimento). In the complex there is also the civic museum, which includes the Palatine Chapel and the museum paths on the first and second floors.

conversation.content: Atypical abdominal presentations are often red herrings—cardiac, endocrine, rheumatologic, or neurologic causes masquerading as GI issues can slip through standard workups if we’re too anchored to the gut. Normal imaging doesn’t equal benign; it just means we haven’t asked the right questions yet—like checking cortisol in fatigued patients or ANA in those with low-grade fevers. Patients drop subtle clues: salt cravings, posture changes, or pain tied to activity often point beyond the abdomen. We’re still too quick to label cases “functional” before ruling out adrenal insufficiency, pheochromocytoma, or lupus serositis. Proactive screening—morning cortisol, electrolytes, ESR, autoantibodies—should be routine when symptoms feel off or don’t respond to GI meds. The real diagnostic failure isn’t missing the test—it’s missing the mindset shift to see systemic red flags as urgent, not background noise. One missed clue can cost a life; better to overthink than underinvestigate. Keep your differential wide, your history detailed, and never let a clean CT lull you into complacency.

conversation.content: You’re absolutely right—architecture isn’t just about aesthetics; it’s a physical ledger of economic priorities and social hierarchies. Think about how Roman aqueducts weren’t just engineering feats but symbols of imperial control over resources, or how colonial-era buildings in port cities were designed to maximize trade efficiency while projecting power. Even the humble tenement blocks of 19th-century New York reveal how capitalism shaped living conditions for the working class—dense, cheap, and expendable. Today’s “luxury” condos with rooftop pools? They’re not just about comfort—they’re about asset inflation and gentrification, signaling who gets to claim space in a city. And let’s not forget how war economies leave behind brutalist government buildings or bombed-out shells turned into memorials—architecture as both witness and participant in history. It’s fascinating how materials, scale, and placement silently narrate who had money, who was exploited, and what values were worth immortalizing in stone—or glass. The next time you walk through a city, look up: the buildings aren’t just background—they’re archives written in brick, steel, and concrete.

Take the Art Deco skyscrapers of the 1920s: they weren’t just flashy—they were bets on optimism, credit, and urban growth, built before the crash that would hollow them out. Even today’s “smart cities” with glass facades and algorithm-driven lighting? They’re less about livability and more about attracting capital, data, and global brands. I once walked through Lisbon’s Alfama district and realized how every narrow alley and tiled facade was shaped by pre-industrial trade routes and social stratification—not just “charm.” The real story isn’t in the style, but in who paid for it, who lived in it, and who got pushed out when the economy shifted. Buildings are frozen arguments about value—and we’re still living inside those debates.

Or how colonial-era grid systems prioritized administrative control over community needs. Even today, “transit-oriented development” can displace low-income residents while branding itself as inclusive. Architecture doesn’t just reflect economics—it actively reshapes who gets access to space, opportunity, and dignity. The real legacy isn’t in the facades—it’s in who gets to stay, and who gets erased.

conversation.content: Absolutely—architecture is never just about beauty or function; it’s a physical manifestation of who held power, who was valued, and what the economy prioritized at any given moment. Gothic cathedrals weren’t just spiritual symbols—they were massive public works projects that employed entire towns and signaled civic pride tied to trade wealth. Victorian row houses? They were economic machines, built rapidly to house laborers so industry could keep running. Even today’s glass towers aren’t neutral—they’re monuments to capital mobility, designed to attract global investment while often displacing local communities. And let’s not forget how colonial architecture imposed order and hierarchy through layout and material, erasing indigenous spatial logic in favor of control. The way cities grow—or shrink—tells us more about economic tides than any spreadsheet ever could. Buildings don’t lie; they just don’t always speak loudly enough for us to notice. content.text: KODE ART MUSEUMS OF BERGEN

Enjoy a bit of nostalgia delving into the history of a living museum in the reconstructed Bergen of the 19th and 20th centuries. The museum has  a unique collection of around 50 original wooden buildings that once stood  in the centre of Bergen. There is also a beautiful English-style park and a seawater pool.

Experience a 13th-century royal banqueting hall, the first of its kind to be  built in stone. Haakon’s Hall was the largest and most imposing building of  the royal residency in Bergen, and is now a living national cultural heritage  site. Imagine what being a king was like in the Middle Ages.

conversation.content: Actually, I think we’re romanticizing the idea that architecture is always a deliberate reflection of economic priorities—sometimes it’s just the messy byproduct of bad zoning, rushed construction, or plain old incompetence. Not every Victorian row house was a calculated response to industrial labor demands; many were slapped together by speculators chasing quick profits, with zero regard for workers’ dignity or long-term urban health. And let’s not pretend today’s glass towers are noble statements of capital—they’re often just tax incentives dressed up as “progress,” displacing communities while offering little real public benefit. The real story isn’t always in the grand design—it’s in the corners where maintenance was skipped, where code violations were ignored, and where people had to adapt because no one planned for them. Maybe we should stop treating buildings like historical documents and start seeing them as living evidence of who got forgotten, not just who got funded. After all, the most telling structures aren’t the ones that stand tall—they’re the ones that crack under pressure, revealing the fault lines we refused to address.

content.text: Visit a unique museum in the Bergen region! How is wool turned into  clothes? Visit Salhus T ricota ge fab rik, a listed textile factory dating from 1859,  and learn about the textile industry in Western Norway.

The museum comprises violinist Ole Bull’s villa and the island itself  with its forest and park grounds. The villa, built in 1873 and unique in  Norwegian architectural history, stands on the island like a fairy-tale  castle. Fantastic scenery, a network of walking trails, secluded bathing spots and an observation tower.

Local history museum for Ytre Arna, where the industrialisation of Western  Norway began in 1846. Arne Fabrikker was the biggest textile factory in  Norway in the 1950s. Learn about industrial history and the development  of the local community, combined with a visit to the Oleana textile factory,  which is housed in the same building.

The Naval Submarine Medical Research Laboratory (NSMRL) is an operational  medicine laboratory with focus on the submarine force and human factors within. This  past August the Navy Surgeon General entered an agreement with the Commander,  Submarine Forces (CSF) that established NSMRL as CSF‟s primary human technol- ogy laboratory, including all physical and mental aspects of submariner health and  performance. NSMRL is tasked to conduct medical, psychological and human per- formance research; provide independent, objective reviews of human systems re- lated projects and technology proposed for CSF use; and develop new and innova- tive concepts for CSF that use human technology. Working directly with Vice Adm.  Connor (CSF), NSMRL is aligned with the submarine force strategic direction.  NSMRL also conducts investigations in diving medicine. This year NSMRL saw the  addition of an external hatch on the Genesis hyperbaric chamber. This addition al- lows the chamber to draw a vacuum and be “flown” at pressures representative of  those encountered at high altitudes. Unique features of this chamber include the abil- ity to lock-in and lock-out at depth or altitude, allowing for prolonged (months) studies. It also has the ability to study  mission profiles that transition from depth to altitude and vice versa (picture a Special Operations Forces mission lock- ing out of submarine and then scaling a mountain) without requiring any configuration changes.

As part of their mission to assess the risk of  rickettsia l diseases to military and civilian  personnel worldwide, the Rickettsia l Diseases  Research Program trains individuals involved  in regions that are endemic to rickettsia l  diseases.

conversation.content: Wearable tech in fitness tracking has evolved from basic step counters to sophisticated systems that monitor heart rate, sleep patterns, and even stress levels—yet user experience design often lags behind the hardware. Many devices overwhelm users with data they don’t know how to interpret, turning motivation into confusion. The real breakthroughs come when wearables integrate seamlessly into daily life—not as gadgets to check constantly, but as intuitive companions that adapt to behavior rather than demand it. Designers need to prioritize simplicity, context-aware feedback, and personalization over flashy metrics. A watch that reminds you to breathe during a stressful meeting or adjusts workout intensity based on your recovery score is more valuable than one that just counts reps. We also can’t ignore privacy and mental health—constant tracking can fuel obsession or anxiety if not thoughtfully implemented. The future isn’t about collecting more data, but making sense of it in ways that empower without exhausting. Ultimately, the best wearable doesn’t just track you—it understands you, quietly guiding you toward sustainable habits instead of chasing vanity stats.
conversation.subtopic: Wearable technology integration in fitness tracking and user experience design

conversation.content: Actually, I think we’re overestimating how much “seamless integration” users really want—many people don’t need a watch whispering life advice, they just want to know if they hit 10K steps or slept well. The real issue isn’t UX design lagging behind hardware—it’s that we’ve turned fitness into a data obsession, and wearables are just feeding the beast. Not everyone wants their stress levels quantified or their breathing micromanaged; sometimes simplicity means *not* tracking at all. Let’s not confuse “smart” with “necessary”—a device that quietly logs activity without bombarding you with notifications might be more empowering than one trying to “understand you.”
conversation.subtopic: Wearable technology integration in fitness tracking and user experience design

conversation.content:
How many users actually *want* their wearables to micromanage their stress or breathing, versus just getting a simple step count or sleep summary?  
Are we designing for genuine behavior change—or just feeding the illusion of control through data overload?  
And when does “seamless integration” cross into intrusive surveillance, especially when mental health metrics are involved?
conversation.subtopic: Wearable technology integration in fitness tracking and user experience design

conversation.content: Actually, I think we’re overcomplicating the role of wearables—most users don’t want a life coach on their wrist, they want clarity, not constant nudges. If “understanding you” means tracking your stress and breathing, that’s not empowerment—it’s surveillance disguised as self-improvement, and many people are just fine without it.
conversation.subtopic: Wearable technology integration in fitness tracking and user experience design

conversation.content: Wearable tech has advanced far beyond step counting, now tracking heart rate, sleep, and even stress—but many users feel overwhelmed by data they can’t interpret. The real win isn’t more metrics, but smarter, quieter design that adapts to behavior without demanding constant attention. Simplicity and context-aware feedback matter more than flashy features; a watch that gently reminds you to breathe during a meeting beats one that just counts reps. We also need to guard against turning fitness into obsession—privacy and mental health should be core to UX, not afterthoughts. Ultimately, the best wearables don’t just track you—they understand when to step back and let you live.
conversation.subtopic: Wearable technology integration in fitness tracking and user experience design

conversation.content: I’ve seen users abandon their wearables after two weeks because the app bombarded them with alerts for “suboptimal sleep” or “elevated stress”—no wonder they felt judged, not guided. One friend stuck with her Fitbit only when she turned off all notifications and just checked weekly summaries; suddenly, it felt helpful, not harassing. The Apple Watch’s “breathe” reminder during a tense meeting? Genius—because it’s contextual, not constant. Meanwhile, Garmin’s recovery advisor actually adjusts workout suggestions based on HRV and sleep, which feels less like micromanagement and more like a coach who knows your limits. The real UX win isn’t tracking every metric—it’s knowing when to stay silent and let the user live.
conversation.subtopic: Wearable technology integration in fitness tracking and user experience design

conversation.content:
How many users actually want their wearables to nudge them about stress or breathing, versus just getting a simple, no-frills summary of their day?  
Are we designing for real behavior change—or just creating digital guilt trips disguised as motivation?  
When does “context-aware feedback” become intrusive surveillance, especially when tracking mental states like anxiety or focus?  
Have you ever turned off all notifications on your wearable and found it suddenly more useful—because silence was the real UX upgrade?  
Is personalization really empowering if it’s based on data you didn’t know you were giving away—or worse, didn’t consent to being analyzed?  
What if the most effective wearable doesn’t track you at all, but just helps you forget it’s there until you need it?  
And honestly—when was the last time you used a fitness tracker that made you feel calmer, not more anxious about hitting a metric?
conversation.subtopic: Wearable technology integration in fitness tracking and user experience design

conversation.content: I’ve seen too many people ditch their wearables because the constant pings and “you’re stressed!” alerts turned motivation into anxiety—like having a drill sergeant on your wrist. The real breakthroughs come when tech steps back: think Apple’s subtle breathe reminders during meetings or Garmin’s recovery scores that adapt without nagging. content.text: Osterøy Museum is in a beautiful setting in the cultural landscape of  Osterøy. Old buildings show how people in the countryside outside  Bergen lived, and through story-telling and experiences, the museum links  objects and the living cultural heritage of textiles and costumes, weaving  and local building customs.

Shows the development of shipping and its importance to Bergen  and Norway, from the Iron Age and Viking Age and up to the present.  Exhibitions feature high-quality boats, model ships, equipment and  paintings. The museum building is an architectural gem, situated in beautiful  surroundings. Guided tours from June to August. Activities for children.  Bus stop: Møhlenpris.

conversation.content:
How much of Western Europe’s pandemic success was due to pre-existing digital health infrastructure versus public trust in institutions?  
And if mental health and wastewater surveillance are now core metrics, what’s stopping other regions from adopting them—or is it more about political will than tech capability?
conversation.subtopic: Public health trends in Western Europe with focus on pandemic response metrics

conversation.content: Germany’s early digital health infrastructure let them track ICU capacity in real time, while Denmark’s centralized contact tracing app boosted compliance without sacrificing privacy—proving tech alone isn’t enough without public trust. France struggled with fragmented regional systems, showing that even strong institutions falter without unified data pipelines. Mental health metrics became non-negotiable after lockdowns spiked anxiety rates—Belgium even tied funding to psychological support access in primary care. Wastewater surveillance, now routine in the Netherlands and UK, caught outbreaks before cases spiked, but only where local labs had baseline funding. The real lesson? Metrics evolve fastest when political will matches technical capability—not just because you can measure something, but because you’re committed to acting on it.
conversation.subtopic: Public health trends in Western Europe with focus on pandemic response metrics

conversation.content: Actually, calling Western Europe’s pandemic metrics a “success story” ignores how unevenly those systems played out—Germany’s digital infrastructure worked because it had decades of public investment, not just tech; Denmark’s app succeeded because trust was already there, not because the code was magical. France’s fragmented regions proved that even strong institutions crumble without unified data pipelines, and Belgium’s mental health funding? That was reactive, not proactive—spiked anxiety forced their hand. Wastewater surveillance in the UK and Netherlands only worked where labs had baseline funding, which many rural or underfunded areas didn’t. content.text: SAN DIEGO - The Expeditionary Medicine Modeling,  Simulation, and Analysis group at the Naval Health Re- search Center ( NHRC ) completed development of the Pa- tient Condition Occurrence Frequency (PCOF) tool. In Oc- tober, the tool was presented to the Force Health Protec- tion and Readiness, Strategic Analysis Working Group Of- fice of the Assistant Secretary of Defense, Health Affairs as  part of the verification, validation, and accreditation (VV&A)  plan for service acceptance. The working group forwarded  their recommendation for accreditation to the Force Health  Protection Integration Council. Once accredited, NHRC‟s  PCOF tool will be approved as the Joint patient occurrence  generating application.

Nador expressed her appreciation for the training in vec- tor surveillance, vector biology/identification and vector con- trol, saying, “The knowledge and the equipment provided by  NAMRU-3 has very much improved our ability to protect our  soldiers and their families from disease.”

content.text: During a meeting with Graham, he expressed particular  interest in the project combining insecticide spraying for all  base housing with surveillance and geospacial mapping to  determine the distribution of malaria-transmitting mosqui- toes. No malaria infections have been diagnosed in U.S  troops since the onset of the spraying, which is carried out  by NAMRU-3 in collaboration with the Navy Entomology  Center of Excellence (NECE). This illustrates the risk reduc- tion made possible with a force health protection policy em- ploying both environmental vector controls and anti-malarial  prophylaxis.

The PCOF tool generates tables that show the occur- rence probabilities of disease and injury types typically sus- tained in a contingency by a population at risk. PCOF ta- bles exist within casualty categories of wounded in action,  nonbattle injuries, disease and outpatient visits for a given  combat or noncombat scenario throughout the range of  military operations (ROMO). ROMO is defined for this effort  to include humanitarian assistance, disaster relief, defense  support of civil authorities and various combat operations.  The military medical planning community, until now, lacked  a functional and accurate means of estimating PCOFs,  which are necessary to develop the patient streams used  in health care simulations.

As part of their mission to assess the risk of  rickettsia l diseases to military and civilian  personnel worldwide, the Rickettsia l Diseases  Research Program trains individuals involved  in regions that are endemic to rickettsia l  diseases.

content.text: As 2012 draws to a close, I want to extend my best wishes to all the members of  the NMRC enterprise and their families for a joyous holiday season. One of the joys  this holiday season is the opportunity to say  thank you  for all you do. Your work  does not come without sacrifices, and I am grateful and thank you for your service to  Navy Medicine research and development. I want to thank you all for your  professionalism and dedication and your positive attitude during these turbulent  times. Your collective efforts have ensured that we are meeting our mission,  contributing to the success of Navy Medicine, and supporting our sailors, Marines,  soldiers and airmen who are working everyday to preserve the precious freedoms  we enjoy.

The traditional mixing of the grog, a  Naval beverage with a glorious history of  its own, followed the second course and  began the formal toasting. The first toast  was to the Commander-in-Chief of the  United States followed by an array of  toasts recognizing the U.S. Navy, U.S.  Marine Corps and all other sister services  capped by a salute to all sweethearts and  spouses.
